headline: Brent trades near $89.80 overnight after Washington rebuffed Iran's reopening conditions, September pricing tilts back toward a hike at 44%, and the 10-year yield sits at 4.72% with tomorrow's consumer-price report left to decide which trade wins.
stance: Monday ran Friday's jobs trade in reverse, and oil did the pushing: Brent settled at $87.85 — up from $82.27 at Friday's close — and traded near $89.80 overnight (~5am ET) after President Trump dismissed Iran's conditions for reopening the Strait of Hormuz, which now run to sanctions relief, unfrozen assets, a US force withdrawal and war reparations. Rates followed: the 10-year Treasury yield closed at 4.72% (4.65% Friday), the 2-year at 4.25% (4.19%), and by this morning prediction-market pricing put 56% on a September hold and 44% on a quarter-point hike — from roughly 65% and 33% Sunday afternoon. The first Fed voice after the payrolls shock leaned the same way: Cleveland's Beth Hammack, who dissented in July in favor of a hike, said Monday that "one 25 basis point move probably doesn't do a whole lot for the economy." Equities barely reacted — the S&P 500 slipped 0.1% to 7,753.11, just below Friday's record close — leaving tomorrow's 8:30am consumer-price report (forecasts near +0.1–0.2% headline, +0.2% core) to settle whether July's jobs contraction or $89 oil is the story that sticks.

news.head: Oil unwound the rate-relief trade
news.body: Brent settled Monday at $87.85, up from $82.27 at Friday's close, and traded near $89.80 overnight (~5am ET), up a further 2.4%; US crude settled at $82.30 and traded near $84.28. The push came after President Trump dismissed Iran's conditions for reopening Hormuz — sanctions relief, unfrozen assets, a US force withdrawal, war reparations — while traffic through the strait ran at 8–15 vessels a day in early August against roughly 130 before the war.

news.head: September tilted back toward a hike
news.body: Prediction-market pricing this morning puts 56% on the Fed holding at the September 16 meeting and 44% on a quarter-point hike — from roughly 65% and 33% Sunday afternoon. No new US data landed in between: the repricing was energy. The payrolls-built hold case lasted one session against rising crude.

news.head: First Fed voice after the jobs shock was hawkish
news.body: Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack — who dissented at July's meeting in favor of a hike — said Monday that "one 25 basis point move probably doesn't do a whole lot for the economy," argued the current 3.50–3.75% setting is not restrictive enough, and said businesses are not signaling restraint on investment plans.

news.head: Metals pressed higher; the yen broke to a new extreme
news.body: Gold closed Monday at $4,448.60, up from Friday's $4,401.30 — a second straight session at the top of its three-year range (87th percentile) — and silver rose to $65.88 from $63.80. The yen weakened to ¥159.22 per dollar at Monday's close from ¥157.75 Friday, a fresh three-year-range extreme, and traded near ¥159.35 overnight despite last week's warning from Japan's finance minister that authorities "would not hesitate" to step in.

news.head: Stocks marked time just under records
news.body: The S&P 500 eased 0.1% Monday to 7,753.11 — just below Friday's record close — with the Dow down 0.1% at 53,975.98 and the Nasdaq down 0.3% at 26,605.36. The VIX rose to 15.46 from Friday's 14.9, still low. Overnight (~5am ET), S&P 500 and Dow futures sat about 0.1% lower; Asia was mixed, with Seoul up 0.7% and Hong Kong down 1.1%.

news.head: Monday's insider filings: smaller, single-buyer purchases
news.body: The newest filings, dated Monday, show about $1.6 million bought at TISI by a single insider, $900,000 across two filings at CLVT, and $618,000 at COE — a quieter tape than the multi-buyer clusters at BRVE and ATTO in Friday's filings.

implications: The September call is now an oil call: hike odds rose 11 points in a day with no new inflation data — pure energy pass-through fear. Tomorrow's report is forecast near +0.1–0.2% headline and +0.2% core; a print in that range keeps the hold case alive, while visible energy effects with Brent near $90 would likely complete the swing back toward a hike.

The bond market is treating this as an inflation problem, not a growth problem: the 10-year yield rose 7 basis points Monday while the 10-year breakeven inflation rate climbed to 2.29% from 2.25% and the 10-year real yield to 2.43% from 2.40%. A growth scare would have pushed those the other way.

Gold's rally now carries positioning risk: the latest weekly futures data shows speculators extended long — the 87th percentile of the past three years, up 32 percentile points in a week — just as the price reached a fresh range extreme. Extended longs are potential sellers on a cool inflation print or a real Hormuz reopening.

Equities still hold their contrarian cushion — bullish bets on Nasdaq 100 futures remain near three-year lows in the same weekly data, unchanged from yesterday's report — but with the VIX at 15.46, protection is thin for a two-sided event like tomorrow's inflation print with oil near $90.

watch.head: Tomorrow's consumer-price report, 8:30am ET
watch.body: The decider for September. Forecasts center near +0.1–0.2% headline and +0.2% core; what matters most is visible energy pass-through. A benign print keeps the hold case alive at these odds — a hot one, with Brent near $90, likely flips the lean back to a hike.

watch.head: CoreWeave after today's close
watch.body: The week's first big test of AI-infrastructure demand: consensus is about $2.55 billion in revenue and a loss of about $1.23 a share, with attention on how fast the $99.4 billion contract backlog converts into revenue. Cisco and Applied Materials follow later this week.

watch.head: Proof, again, on the strait
watch.body: Brent has gone from $82.27 at Friday's close to near $89.80 overnight on conditions and rebuffs alone. Transits are still running 8–15 vessels a day against roughly 130 pre-war; only free tanker movement or a published, verifiable agreement settles the oil question in either direction.

watch.head: Today's smaller data
watch.body: Small-business optimism at 6am ET and existing-home sales at 10am — secondary to tomorrow's inflation report, but the first read on whether July's payrolls contraction is showing up in confidence.

sections.title: Macro & Rates
bullets: The biggest change since yesterday morning: the September hold case built on Friday's payrolls contraction lost ground to oil. Prediction-market pricing this morning puts 56% on a hold and 44% on a quarter-point hike — from roughly 65% and 33% Sunday afternoon — with no new US data in between; crude did the repricing.

Brent settled Monday at $87.85 — up from $82.27 at Friday's close — and traded near $89.80 overnight (~5am ET), up a further 2.4%, after President Trump dismissed Iran's reopening conditions; US crude settled at $82.30 and traded near $84.28 overnight. Traffic through the strait ran 8–15 vessels a day in early August versus roughly 130 before the war.

Treasuries gave back the payrolls rally: the 10-year yield closed Monday at 4.72% (4.65% Friday), the 2-year at 4.25% (4.19%), with the curve near +47 basis points. The move reads as inflation rather than growth: the 10-year breakeven inflation rate rose to 2.29% from 2.25% and the 10-year real, inflation-adjusted yield to 2.43% from 2.40%.

Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack — the July dissenter in favor of a hike — said Monday that "one 25 basis point move probably doesn't do a whole lot for the economy" and that the current 3.50–3.75% policy setting is not restrictive enough. She was the first official to speak after Friday's jobs report.

Gold closed at $4,448.60, up from $4,401.30 Friday — a second straight session at the top of its three-year range (87th percentile) — with silver at $65.88 from $63.80. The yen weakened to ¥159.22 at Monday's close from ¥157.75 Friday, a fresh three-year-range extreme (89th percentile), and traded near ¥159.35 overnight despite last week's intervention warnings from Tokyo.

Extended longs are potential sellers if the inflation or Hormuz story breaks the other way.

sections.title: Equity Markets
bullets: Monday's close: S&P 500 down 0.1% at 7,753.11 — just below Friday's record close — Dow down 0.1% at 53,975.98, Nasdaq down 0.3% at 26,605.36. Overnight (~5am ET), S&P 500 and Dow futures sat about 0.1% lower; Asia was mixed, with Seoul up 0.7% and Hong Kong down 1.1%.
Protection stayed thin into tomorrow's inflation report: the VIX closed Monday at 15.46, up from 14.9 Friday but still low, and its Nasdaq-100 counterpart closed at 23.04.
Breadth softened with the tape: 65.3% of S&P 500 members closed above their 50-day trend line, from about 68% Friday; 55% of Nasdaq-100 members did, from 62%.

CoreWeave reports after today's close — consensus is about $2.55 billion in revenue and a loss of about $1.23 a share, with attention on how fast its $99.4 billion contract backlog converts into revenue — the week's first big read on AI-infrastructure demand, with Cisco and Applied Materials later in the week.

Monday's newest insider filings were smaller and mostly single-buyer: about $1.6 million at TISI, $900,000 across two filings at CLVT, and $618,000 at COE — a quieter tape than the multi-buyer clusters in Friday's filings.
sections.positioning: Unchanged background from the latest weekly futures data: bullish bets in Nasdaq 100 futures sit at the 1st percentile of the past three years — skepticism, not exuberance, underneath a tape just off its record — with hedgers at the opposite extreme.

single_name.note: (Taiwan Semiconductor, the world's largest contract chipmaker) — a fresh insider purchase was filed Monday, the shares trade above their 200-day trend line, and the setup's dark-pool and options signals are both live; it has been on the scan list since mid-June.

sections.title: Credit & Liquidity
bullets: Credit ignored the oil move through the latest data (spread data runs a day behind): the high-yield-over-investment-grade spread was 270 basis points in Friday's data, from 271 Thursday, with investment-grade spreads at 78 basis points.

The hedging ahead of tomorrow's report is happening in Treasuries rather than stocks: the MOVE index — the Treasury market's version of the VIX — closed Monday at 75.5, up from 72 Friday, while the VIX rose about half a point.
Short-term funding stayed quiet: the key bank-funding spreads sat near -1 basis point and the commercial-paper funding spread at 21 basis points in Friday's data.

The system's spare-cash cushion is still gone: the overnight reverse-repo facility held $1 billion Monday, with bank reserves at $2,993.3 billion and the Treasury's cash account at $907.3 billion in Wednesday's weekly snapshot.
sections.positioning: Primary-dealer high-yield inventory remains mid-range — the 35th percentile of its three-year span, unchanged — no stress signal on either side of the credit book.
